sections.title: The organism: Brucella species, hosts and epidemiology

blocks.text: Brucellosis (also called **Malta fever** or **undulant fever**) is a **zoonosis**: the infection is maintained in livestock and humans are accidental hosts. The cause is **Brucella**, a **Gram-negative coccobacillus** that survives and multiplies **inside host cells**.

blocks.title: Human-pathogenic Brucella species
rows: Most severe illness; the usual cause of chronic brucellosis and of brucella arthritis; highest blood-culture yield
Blood cultures positive in only about half of cases
The fourth species that infects humans

blocks.title: Epidemiology
items: Highest incidence: **Mediterranean basin, Middle East** and the tropics; roughly half a million new cases a year worldwide.
The UK is officially free of animal brucellosis, so UK cases are imported; it is a **notifiable disease** there.
Brucella is on the short list of infections to consider in a **febrile traveller from the Middle East** (with MERS).
Davidson lists Brucella among geographically restricted causes of fever (Africa, Asia, Central and South America).

blocks.text: Because Brucella persists for long periods **within the reticulo-endothelial system**, the disease tends to become **chronic and to relapse**, even after antibiotics. This is why treatment uses **prolonged combination therapy**.
Washington's Manual names three species (melitensis, abortus, suis); Davidson names **four**, adding **B. canis** from dogs. Follow Davidson: four species cause human disease.

Most people are infected **by mouth**: unpasteurised milk and other dairy products, or uncooked meat and offal. Infected animals can keep shedding the organism in their milk for long periods. **Occupational exposure** is also common, and spread between people is **rare**.

blocks.title: Routes of infection
rows: Unpasteurised milk and dairy products; raw meat, offal
Households and travellers in endemic areas
Animal urine, faeces, vaginal discharge, placenta and uterine products
Splash or aerosol to the conjunctiva or respiratory tract
Animal birth products and body fluids; laboratory cultures
Listed as a less frequent portal of entry

blocks.title: What happens after entry
items: Organisms pass along **lymphatics** to regional lymph nodes.
They then spread through the **bloodstream**.
They finally settle in the **reticulo-endothelial system**, which explains the lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

blocks.title: Prevention
items: **Pasteurise milk** and avoid unpasteurised dairy products (this is also the advice in pregnancy, where infection may raise fetal loss).
Practise good hygiene when handling infected animals.
**Vaccinate animals** to eradicate the infection from herds.
There is **no human vaccine**.

blocks.text: Read the occupation in the stem. A **farmer, shepherd, vet, abattoir worker or butcher** with prolonged fever and sweats should make you think of brucellosis.
**Warn the laboratory** whenever brucellosis is suspected. Brucella can infect laboratory staff, so cultures must be handled at the correct biosafety level.

sections.title: Clinical features: acute, chronic and localised disease

blocks.text: Davidson gives an incubation period of **5–30 days**. Onset is often **insidious**, with malaise, weakness, headache, generalised aches and **night sweats**. The fever is classically **undulant** (waves of fever separated by afebrile spells), though continuous or intermittent patterns also occur.

blocks.title: Three clinical pictures
rows: High swinging fever, rigors, sweats (which may be malodorous), lethargy, headache, joint and muscle pain, back pain, scrotal pain; sometimes delirium, abdominal pain, constipation
Non-specific: lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; splenomegaly may cause thrombocytopenia
Easy fatigue, myalgia, recurrent bouts of fever, depression
About **30%** of patients; more likely when diagnosis and treatment are late

blocks.title: Focal complications by system
items: **Bones and joints:** suppurative arthritis, synovitis, bursitis, osteomyelitis, **sacroiliitis**, **spinal spondylitis**, paravertebral or **psoas abscess**.
**Nervous system:** meningitis, intracranial or subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke, myelopathy, radiculopathy, cranial nerve palsies.
**Eye:** uveitis, retinal thrombophlebitis.
**Heart:** **endocarditis** (often the **aortic valve**), myocarditis.
**Lung:** pneumonitis or abscess, hilar lymphadenopathy.
**Abdomen:** hepatitis, splenic abscess or calcification.
**Genitourinary:** **epididymo-orchitis**.
**Blood:** pancytopenia.

blocks.note: Look at: the body map of brucellosis features, organised by organ system (joints and spine, nervous system, eye, heart, lung, liver, spleen, testis, blood).

blocks.title: Osteoarticular disease, the commonest focal form
items: **Young patients:** sacroiliitis is typical.
**Older patients:** spondylodiscitis or peripheral arthritis is typical.
Brucella arthritis is usually a **migratory mono- or oligoarthritis of large joints**. It may be septic or reactive and is commoner when infection has lasted over 6 months.
Davidson's rheumatology chapter describes the sequence: an acute febrile illness first, then focal arthritis, bursitis, osteomyelitis, sacroiliitis or a paravertebral/psoas abscess in some patients.

blocks.title: Where brucellosis appears in differential lists
items: Pyrexia of unknown origin (infections cause 20–40% of PUO).
Generalised lymphadenopathy (with TB, leptospirosis, syphilis, atypical mycobacteria).
Moderate splenomegaly from chronic infection (with TB).
Infective arthritis due to unusual organisms (with Lyme disease, Salmonella, Mycoplasma).

blocks.text: **Malodorous, mouldy-smelling sweat** is described as almost pathognomonic of brucellosis.
Exam pattern: **weeks of fever, a fever-free gap of several days, then fever again** (undulant), with lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, suggests brucellosis.

The blood count tends to fall, not rise. Expect **thrombocytopenia** (from splenomegaly), **neutropenia** or **pancytopenia**; monocytosis can occur. The sources list Brucella under **neutropenia**, not under causes of a raised neutrophil count.
Incubation figures differ: Davidson **5–30 days**, Kumar 1–3 weeks, and KC Essentials puts brucellosis in both its medium (10–21 days) and long (>21 days) groups. Quote Davidson's range.
**Depression** is a recognised feature of chronic brucellosis (Kumar). Do not reject it as a feature in a 'which is not a feature' question.

The **definitive (gold-standard) test is culture** of Brucella from blood or tissue. Cultures need **prolonged incubation**, and the laboratory must be told so that staff are protected. Serology supports the diagnosis but has limitations.

blocks.title: Tests and what they add
rows: B. melitensis: positive in **75–80%**; B. abortus: about **50%**
Raises the yield if antibiotics were given before cultures
Main route to diagnosis in localised disease
Antibody titres are often **low** in focal disease
Endemic areas: a **single titre >1/320** or a **fourfold rise** supports acute infection
Takes **weeks** to turn positive, then detects ~95% of acute cases; can cross-react with **Francisella tularensis**
Raised in current or recent infection
A negative result excludes chronic non-localised disease
No standardised molecular test for routine use

blocks.title: Clinical situations that should prompt Brucella testing
items: **Pyrexia of unknown origin** (fever for over 2 weeks without a diagnosis): Brucella serology is considered case by case with Coxiella and Bartonella.
**Bone marrow biopsy in PUO** (yield up to 15%) can identify brucellosis; send marrow for **culture as well as microscopy**.
**Culture-negative endocarditis:** Brucella is one of the fastidious causes, with HACEK organisms, Coxiella, Bartonella and Tropheryma whipplei; serology helps.
Unexplained **neutropenia** or **monocytosis** in a febrile patient with animal exposure.

blocks.text: An early negative serology does not exclude acute brucellosis, because antibodies take weeks to appear. Take **blood cultures first** and repeat serology later.

The serology cut-offs differ between sources. **Davidson:** in endemic areas, a single titre above **1/320** or a fourfold rise. **Kumar:** a fourfold or greater rise to above **1/160** over 4 weeks is highly suggestive. Use Davidson's figure; Kumar adds that serology is most useful in chronic disease.
Kumar gives a single blood-culture yield of **50%** in the acute phase (higher with B. melitensis). Davidson splits it by species: **75–80% melitensis, 50% abortus**. Quote Davidson.

Brucellosis is always treated with a **combination** of antibiotics given for a **long course**. Aminoglycosides act **synergistically with tetracyclines** against Brucella, and the organism's long survival inside cells explains why the disease tends to relapse, even after treatment.

blocks.title: Davidson regimens (Box 11.40)
rows: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily orally **plus** gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV once daily
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily **with** oral rifampicin 600–900 mg once daily (all oral)
Doxycycline + rifampicin **plus** gentamicin; **or** ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily + rifampicin
6 weeks (gentamicin 7 days); or 3 months for ciprofloxacin + rifampicin
6 weeks; ceftriaxone until the CSF clears (confirm susceptibility)
Usually **surgery**, plus doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole, with gentamicin
4 weeks; caution in the final week of pregnancy

blocks.text: The pregnancy regimen (rifampicin + co-trimoxazole) needs caution in the **last week of pregnancy**: the drugs can displace bilirubin from albumin, with a risk of **kernicterus** in the fetus.
**Endocarditis** has the longest and heaviest regimen: surgery in almost every case, three oral drugs for 6 months, and gentamicin for 2–4 weeks.

Other books give different first-line choices. **Kumar:** triple therapy with doxycycline, rifampicin and an aminoglycoside (usually gentamicin). **Washington:** doxycycline for 6 weeks (12 weeks in osteoarticular disease) plus IM streptomycin for the first 2–3 weeks, with rifampin, fluoroquinolones or co-trimoxazole as alternatives. For exams, quote Davidson's regimens.
Single-drug or short courses are wrong answers. Every regimen in the sources combines at least two drugs for **at least 4 weeks**, and most run 6 weeks or longer.

cards.back: **Brucella** spp.: a **Gram-negative, intracellular coccobacillus**; the disease is a zoonosis.

cards.front: Brucella species and their animal hosts?
cards.back: **B. melitensis**: goats, sheep, camels. **B. abortus**: cattle. **B. suis**: pigs. **B. canis**: dogs.

cards.front: Which Brucella species causes the most severe disease, and which forms abscesses?
cards.back: **B. melitensis** causes the most severe disease; **B. suis** tends to form abscesses.

cards.front: Why does brucellosis relapse and become chronic?
cards.back: The organism survives for long periods **inside cells of the reticulo-endothelial system**, even after antibiotics.

cards.front: Commonest route of human Brucella infection?
cards.back: **Ingestion**: unpasteurised milk and dairy products, raw meat or offal.
Animal fluids or birth products through **abraded skin**; splashes or aerosols to the **conjunctiva or respiratory tract** (including laboratory exposure). Person-to-person spread is rare.

cards.front: Is there a human vaccine against brucellosis?
cards.back: **No.** Prevention relies on animal vaccination, milk pasteurisation and hygiene when handling animals.

cards.front: What proportion of brucellosis patients develop localised infection?
cards.back: About **30%**, more often when diagnosis and treatment are delayed.

cards.front: Symptom described as almost pathognomonic of brucellosis?
Typical osteoarticular site of brucellosis by age?
cards.back: Young patients: **sacroiliitis**. Older patients: **spondylodiscitis** or peripheral arthritis.
**75–80%** for B. melitensis, about **50%** for B. abortus. CSF culture is positive in about 30% of neurobrucellosis.

cards.front: Serological criterion for acute brucellosis in endemic areas (Davidson)?
cards.back: A single titre **above 1/320** or a **fourfold rise** in titre.

cards.front: Davidson first-line regimen for non-localised brucellosis in adults?
cards.back: **Doxycycline 100 mg bd for 6 weeks + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily for 7 days**, or doxycycline + rifampicin, both for 6 weeks.
Usually **surgery**, plus doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for **6 months**, with gentamicin for 2–4 weeks.
**Rifampicin + co-trimoxazole for 4 weeks**; take care in the final week (bilirubin displacement, risk of kernicterus).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old shepherd from a Mediterranean island regularly drinks raw sheep's milk. He has had 5 weeks of fever that comes and goes, with drenching sweats and an enlarged liver and spleen. After prolonged incubation, his blood culture grows Gram-negative coccobacilli.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Sheep's milk, an undulant fever with sweats, hepatosplenomegaly and a **Gram-negative coccobacillus** that needed long incubation all point to **Brucella**. Sheep and goats carry **B. melitensis**, the species that causes the most severe disease.
whyNot: Typhoid is acquired from human carriers through contaminated food and water; the sheep's milk and the coccobacillary morphology fit Brucella.
Listeria is linked to unpasteurised soft cheeses and mainly affects pregnant women, neonates, the elderly and the immunocompromised; sheep contact with an undulant fever fits Brucella.
Leptospira is a spirochaete caught from water contaminated by animal urine; it does not grow as a coccobacillus in routine blood culture.
Borrelia is a tick-borne spirochaete that causes Lyme disease, not a milk-borne coccobacillus.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old pig farmer from South Asia has fever, night sweats and left upper quadrant pain. CT shows a splenic abscess, and Brucella is grown from the aspirate.
questions.leadIn: Which Brucella species is most likely?
questions.explanation: **B. suis** comes from **pigs** (Davidson specifies South Asia) and is particularly associated with **abscess formation**. Both clues point the same way.
whyNot: B. melitensis comes from goats, sheep and camels and causes the most severe disease, but abscess formation is the hallmark of B. suis.
B. abortus is acquired from cattle.
B. canis is acquired from dogs.
Francisella is a different genus. Its antibodies can cross-react with Brucella serology, but here Brucella itself was grown.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops fever and sweats 3 weeks after returning from a village holiday in the Middle East. She stayed with a family who kept goats and ate their home-made fresh cheese every day. Nobody else at home is unwell.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mode of acquisition?
options: Ingestion of an unpasteurised dairy product
Respiratory droplets from an infected person
questions.explanation: Brucellosis is mostly caught by **eating or drinking unpasteurised dairy products** from infected goats, sheep or cattle. Infected animals shed the organism in milk for long periods. Spread between people is rare.
whyNot: Mosquitoes transmit malaria and arboviruses, not Brucella.
Ticks transmit Borrelia (Lyme disease) and rickettsiae, not Brucella.
Person-to-person transmission of brucellosis is rare.
Freshwater exposure is linked to schistosomiasis and leptospirosis.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old veterinary surgeon who works with cattle and goats has 3 weeks of swinging fever, sweats and back pain. The admitting doctor suspects brucellosis and is about to send blood cultures.
questions.leadIn: Which action is most important when sending the cultures?
options: Tell the laboratory that brucellosis is suspected
Start doxycycline first, then take the cultures
Ask for cultures to be discarded if there is no growth at 48 hours
Send serology instead and defer cultures
Send a throat swab in place of blood cultures
questions.explanation: Brucella can **infect laboratory staff**, so the laboratory must be **warned** and must culture the specimen at the proper biosafety level. The warning also prompts the **prolonged incubation** this slow-growing organism needs.
whyNot: Cultures should come first: Davidson notes that once antibiotics have been given, bone marrow culture may be needed to raise the yield.
Brucella cultures need prolonged incubation; discarding at 48 hours would miss it.
Culture is the definitive test, and serology takes weeks to become positive.
A throat swab has no role; culture of blood or tissue is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old camel herder has had 6 weeks of fever that settles for several days at a time and then returns. He has heavy sweats with a mouldy smell and pain in the right buttock. Pressing on the pelvis reproduces the buttock pain, and he has small lymph nodes and a palpable spleen.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Animal contact, an **undulant fever**, **malodorous sweat** (almost pathognomonic), lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly point to brucellosis. **Sacroiliitis** is the typical focal bone lesion in young patients.
whyNot: Ankylosing spondylitis causes sacroiliitis but not swinging fever, foul sweats, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
Mycobacterial bone infection is typically axial (Pott's disease); the livestock exposure, undulant pattern and mouldy-smelling sweat favour Brucella.
Typhoid is suggested by fever with constipation, rash and relative bradycardia, not by sacroiliitis and foul sweats.
Infectious mononucleosis presents with sore throat, lymphadenopathy and sometimes a rash after ampicillin.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old goat farmer had several months of intermittent fever before brucellosis was diagnosed. He now has worsening breathlessness and a new early diastolic murmur heard best along the left sternal border.
questions.leadIn: Which focal complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Localised disease affects about 30% of patients and is more likely when **diagnosis is delayed**. Brucella endocarditis is linked to **goat or cattle contact** and often involves the **aortic valve**; an early diastolic murmur suggests aortic regurgitation.
whyNot: Epididymo-orchitis causes a painful swollen testis, not a murmur.
Spondylitis causes back pain, not heart failure with a murmur.
Meningitis causes headache and neck stiffness.
Uveitis causes a painful red eye.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old dairy worker has had 2 weeks of fever, sweats and arthralgia. He has had no antibiotics. Brucellosis is suspected.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation gives the definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Culture of the organism** is the gold standard. Blood cultures are positive in most B. melitensis and about half of B. abortus infections, and they need prolonged incubation.
whyNot: Serology only supports the diagnosis. It takes weeks to turn positive, and a single low titre is not diagnostic in endemic areas.
The Widal test is a test for typhoid.
The Paul–Bunnell test is a test for infectious mononucleosis.
Liver biopsy is invasive and is not the test of choice for brucellosis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man living in an endemic rural area has had 10 days of fever and sweats. His Brucella agglutination titre is 1/160. Blood cultures are still incubating.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of the serology?
options: It does not establish acute infection; repeat the titre later and await cultures
It proves cross-reaction with Francisella tularensis
questions.explanation: In **endemic areas**, Davidson requires a single titre **above 1/320** or a **fourfold rise** to support acute infection. Antibodies take **weeks** to appear, so a low early titre neither confirms nor excludes the disease. Paired titres and culture decide.
whyNot: 1/160 is below Davidson's 1/320 threshold for a single titre in endemic areas.
Serology can be negative or low early, so a low titre does not exclude infection.
Localised disease typically gives low titres, but a single titre cannot define it; culture from the affected site is needed.
Cross-reaction with Francisella is possible but cannot be proven from one titre.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has acute brucellosis with fever and splenomegaly but no focal lesions. He is not pregnant, has normal renal function and no drug allergies.
questions.leadIn: Which regimen is recommended by Davidson?
options: Doxycycline for 6 weeks plus gentamicin for the first 7 days
questions.explanation: For **non-localised** disease in adults, Davidson recommends **doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily for 7 days** (or doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks). Aminoglycosides are synergistic with tetracyclines.
whyNot: A single drug for 1 week ignores the need for prolonged combination therapy against an intracellular organism.
Amoxicillin is not part of any brucellosis regimen in the sources.
Ceftriaxone appears only as an add-on for neurobrucellosis.
Ciprofloxacin is used only with rifampicin, for bone disease.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has brucellosis confirmed by blood culture. There is no focal disease.
questions.leadIn: Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for 6 months
questions.explanation: Davidson's pregnancy regimen is **rifampicin + co-trimoxazole for 4 weeks**, with **no doxycycline**. Take care in the final week of pregnancy, because the drugs can displace bilirubin and risk **kernicterus**.
whyNot: The pregnancy regimen leaves out doxycycline.
This regimen contains doxycycline, which the pregnancy regimen avoids.
This is the alternative regimen for bone disease, not the pregnancy regimen.
This is the endocarditis regimen, given with surgery.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old shepherd has had 5 weeks of fever and sweats. A local clinic gave him a week of oral antibiotics, which did not help. Two sets of blood cultures taken since admission are negative, and early serology is equivocal. A bone marrow biopsy is planned for pyrexia of unknown origin.
questions.leadIn: Which use of the marrow sample is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
options: Send the aspirate for Brucella culture as well as microscopy
Send the trephine for histology only
Discard the aspirate if microscopy is normal
Send the aspirate only for cytogenetics
Send the aspirate for a Widal test
questions.explanation: Step 1: animal exposure plus prolonged fever and sweats makes brucellosis likely. Step 2: **prior antibiotics** lower blood-culture yield. Step 3: Davidson says **bone marrow culture**, though not routine, increases the yield in exactly this situation. In PUO work-up, marrow should always go for **culture as well as microscopy**; marrow biopsy in PUO can reveal brucellosis.
whyNot: Histology alone may show non-specific changes; the organism is identified by culture.
Normal microscopy does not exclude infection, and culture is the key step.
Cytogenetics looks for haematological malignancy, not infection.
The Widal test is a serological test for typhoid and is not done on marrow.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old abattoir worker has fever, headache, neck stiffness and a left sixth cranial nerve palsy. Brucella is grown from his CSF.
questions.leadIn: Which regimen does Davidson recommend?
options: Doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks plus IV ceftriaxone until the CSF clears
Doxycycline for 6 weeks plus gentamicin for 7 days
Surgery plus doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for 6 months
questions.explanation: Step 1: cranial nerve palsy with meningism and a positive CSF culture means **neurobrucellosis** (CSF culture is positive in only about 30%). Step 2: Davidson gives this form **doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks plus IV ceftriaxone** until the CSF clears. Step 3: confirm susceptibility, because sensitivity to third-generation cephalosporins varies.
whyNot: This is the regimen for non-localised disease, not neurobrucellosis.
This is the pregnancy regimen.
Monotherapy is never recommended for brucellosis.
This is the endocarditis regimen.

questions.theme: Brucella species and their animal sources
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely organism from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 46-year-old goat herder in Greece has a severe febrile illness. After inadequate treatment it becomes chronic, with a migratory arthritis of the knees and ankles.
items.explanation: Goats point to **B. melitensis**. This species causes the most severe disease and is the commonest cause of **chronic brucellosis and brucella arthritis**, typically a migratory large-joint arthritis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old cattle rancher in Africa has a febrile illness. The doctor warns that a single blood culture is positive in only about half of patients with this species.
items.explanation: Two steps: **cattle** means **B. abortus**, and Davidson quotes a blood-culture yield of about **50%** for B. abortus, against 75–80% for B. melitensis.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man who keeps pigs in South Asia develops fever and a paravertebral abscess.
items.explanation: Pigs and **abscess formation** are the two clues to **B. suis**.

items.stem: A 30-year-old dog breeder develops an undulant fever. Blood cultures grow Brucella, and she has had no contact with farm animals or dairy products.
items.explanation: **B. canis** is the dog-associated species and the fourth Brucella species that infects humans.

questions.theme: Febrile illnesses with animal, food or travel exposure
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 42-year-old veterinary surgeon in Jordan had 3 weeks of fever, then about 10 days without fever, and the fever has now returned. He has profuse, mouldy-smelling sweats, low back pain and hepatosplenomegaly.
items.explanation: An occupational animal exposure, an **undulant** fever pattern, **malodorous sweat** and hepatosplenomegaly is the classic brucellosis picture.

items.stem: A 35-year-old sewage worker develops fever, severe headache, myalgia and red eyes without discharge. A week later he becomes jaundiced and his creatinine rises.
items.explanation: **Conjunctival suffusion** and a two-phase illness that can progress to liver and kidney injury point to **leptospirosis**, which is caught from water contaminated by animal urine.

items.stem: A woman who ate unpasteurised soft cheeses during pregnancy had a flu-like illness. Her baby is born with meningitis.
items.explanation: Two steps: unpasteurised dairy could suggest brucellosis, but **neonatal meningitis** after a flu-like illness in the mother is the classic pattern of **listeriosis**. Davidson lists brucellosis in pregnancy only as possibly increasing fetal loss.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man returned from South Asia 2 weeks ago. He has a step-wise rising fever, constipation, faint rose-coloured spots on the trunk and a pulse slower than expected for his temperature.
items.explanation: Fever with constipation, rash and **relative bradycardia** is the typhoid pattern.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely investigation from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Culture of aspirate from the affected joint or abscess

items.stem: A 31-year-old farmer has had 10 days of swinging fever and sweats after drinking raw goat's milk. He has not had any antibiotics. Which single test is most likely to give the definitive diagnosis?
items.explanation: Culture is the gold standard, and **blood culture** before antibiotics is positive in most B. melitensis infections. It needs **prolonged incubation**.

items.stem: A 47-year-old herdsman had 10 days of antibiotics from a pharmacy before referral. Three sets of blood cultures are negative, but brucellosis remains likely. Which test now offers the best chance of isolating the organism?
items.explanation: Davidson notes that **bone marrow culture**, though not routine, increases yield when **antibiotics were given before cultures**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with known animal exposure has a psoas abscess on CT but few systemic symptoms. His Brucella agglutination titre is low. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Two steps: this is **localised** brucellosis, in which antibody titres are **low**. Kumar says the diagnosis then usually comes from **culture of the involved site**.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has had more than a year of fatigue and myalgia after a brucellosis-like illness. There is no focal lesion. Which test, if negative, excludes chronic non-localised brucellosis?
items.explanation: A raised **Brucella IgG** indicates current or recent infection, and a **negative** result excludes chronic non-localised brucellosis (Kumar).

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely complication from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 21-year-old shepherd with brucellosis has pain deep in the left buttock that is worse when he stands on the left leg and when the pelvis is compressed.
items.explanation: In **young** patients, **sacroiliitis** is the typical focal bone lesion of brucellosis.

items.stem: A 66-year-old retired farmer with weeks of fever has lumbar pain, holds his right hip flexed and has pain on passive hip extension.
items.explanation: Two steps: in **older** patients the spine is the usual site (spondylodiscitis), and a **flexed, painful hip** suggests the infection has tracked into a **psoas abscess**.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man with acute brucellosis develops a painful, swollen and tender right hemiscrotum.
items.explanation: Scrotal pain is a feature of acute brucellosis, and **epididymo-orchitis** is a recognised focal complication.

items.stem: A 55-year-old cattle farmer with prolonged fever has a new aortic regurgitant murmur. Routine blood cultures are negative at 5 days.
items.explanation: Brucella is a cause of **culture-negative endocarditis**, is linked to cattle or goat contact, and often affects the **aortic valve**.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely regimen from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Doxycycline for 6 weeks plus gentamicin for 7 days
Doxycycline plus rifampicin, both for 6 weeks
Doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks plus gentamicin for 7 days
Doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks plus IV ceftriaxone until the CSF clears
Surgery plus doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for 6 months, with gentamicin for 2–4 weeks

items.stem: A 36-year-old man has non-localised brucellosis. He refuses injections and needs an entirely oral regimen.
items.explanation: Davidson offers two regimens for non-localised disease. The **all-oral** one is **doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks**.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has Brucella vertebral osteomyelitis. She had a severe reaction to doxycycline in the past.
items.explanation: Two steps: **bone disease** has two Davidson options. Doxycycline must be avoided, so choose **ciprofloxacin + rifampicin for 3 months**.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has Brucella meningitis confirmed on CSF culture.
items.explanation: For **neurobrucellosis**, add **IV ceftriaxone** to 6 weeks of doxycycline + rifampicin until the CSF clears, after confirming susceptibility.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation has acute brucellosis.
items.explanation: The **pregnancy** regimen is **rifampicin + co-trimoxazole for 4 weeks**, with no doxycycline. Take care in the last week (kernicterus risk).

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely route of acquisition from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Contact of broken skin with animal birth products
Splash of animal fluid into the eye
Inhalation of aerosol from a laboratory culture
Sexual contact with an infected person
Swimming in water contaminated by rat urine

items.stem: A 28-year-old biomedical scientist develops undulant fever 3 weeks after working on a blood culture bottle from a febrile farmer. The request form did not mention brucellosis, so the bottle was opened on the open bench.
items.explanation: Two steps: Brucella readily infects **laboratory workers**, which is why the lab must be warned. An unflagged culture handled outside the right biosafety containment points to **aerosol exposure**.

items.stem: A 45-year-old vet with cracked, ungloved hands helped deliver a stillborn calf and handled the placenta. Three weeks later she has fever and sweats.
items.explanation: Animal **uterine products and vaginal discharge** can transmit Brucella through **abraded skin**.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man from a Middle Eastern village says that his family traditionally eat raw sheep's liver at festivals. He presents with prolonged fever and splenomegaly.
items.explanation: Besides dairy products, Brucella is acquired from **uncooked meat or offal**.

items.stem: Two children in a goat-keeping household develop fever and arthralgia. The family drink milk straight from their own goats.
items.explanation: **Unpasteurised milk** is the commonest source; infected animals shed Brucella in milk for long periods.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old dairy farmer has had 4 weeks of undulant fever and sweats. He has splenomegaly, and Brucella is grown from his blood.
questions.leadIn: Which full blood count pattern is most consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Low counts of all three cell lines (pancytopenia)
questions.explanation: Brucellosis tends to **lower** blood counts. Splenomegaly can cause **thrombocytopenia**, Brucella is a recognised infectious cause of **neutropenia** (and monocytosis), and **pancytopenia** is listed among its complications.
whyNot: Leucocytosis is not typical; the sources list neutropenia as the Brucella pattern.
Eosinophilia suggests parasites or allergy, not brucellosis.
Polycythaemia is not a feature of brucellosis.
Splenomegaly in brucellosis lowers the platelet count rather than raising it.

questions.stem: A public-health team is planning how to reduce human brucellosis in a rural district where many families keep goats and sheep.
questions.leadIn: Which measure is most appropriate?
options: Vaccinating all villagers with a human Brucella vaccine
questions.explanation: Prevention relies on **pasteurising milk**, **vaccinating animals** to eradicate infection, and hygiene when handling animals. There is **no human vaccine**.
whyNot: No vaccine is available for humans.
Brucella is not spread by mosquitoes.
Person-to-person spread is rare, so isolating patients is not useful.
The organism comes from animal products, not faecally contaminated water.

questions.theme: Key numbers in the diagnosis of brucellosis (Davidson)
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely figure from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman who keeps goats and sheep has acute brucellosis. What proportion of patients infected with this species have positive blood cultures?
items.explanation: Two steps: goats and sheep mean **B. melitensis**. Davidson gives a blood-culture positivity of **75–80%** for this species.

items.stem: A 55-year-old cattle farmer has acute brucellosis. What proportion of patients infected with the cattle species have positive blood cultures?
items.explanation: Cattle mean **B. abortus**. Its blood cultures are positive in about **50%** of cases.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has suspected neurobrucellosis. In what proportion of such patients is the CSF culture positive?
items.explanation: CSF culture is positive in only about **30%** of neurobrucellosis, so a negative culture does not exclude it.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man's first Brucella serology is negative after 1 week of fever. What proportion of acute infections does serology eventually detect?
items.explanation: Serology is slow to turn positive (several weeks), but it should eventually detect about **95%** of acute infections. Repeat it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old goat farmer has Brucella endocarditis of the aortic valve with a large vegetation and progressive heart failure.
questions.leadIn: Which management plan does Davidson recommend?
options: Valve surgery plus doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for 6 months, with gentamicin for 2–4 weeks
Doxycycline plus gentamicin for 7 days with no surgery
Doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks with no surgery
questions.explanation: Brucella endocarditis **almost always needs surgery**. The antibiotics are doxycycline, rifampicin and co-trimoxazole for **6 months**, with gentamicin for the first **2–4 weeks**.
whyNot: This short course is for non-localised disease, and endocarditis almost always needs surgery.
A 6-week oral regimen without surgery is the regimen for non-localised disease.
This is the pregnancy regimen.
This is an option for bone disease.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 37-year-old camel herder from the Arabian Peninsula has had fever on and off for 2 months, with low back pain, mouldy-smelling night sweats, generalised small lymph nodes and a moderately enlarged spleen.
items.explanation: An **undulant** fever with **malodorous sweats**, back pain, generalised lymphadenopathy and moderate splenomegaly in a camel herder means brucellosis (B. melitensis also infects camels).

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has fever, blurred vision and enlarged cervical lymph nodes.
items.explanation: Fever with **visual symptoms** and lymphadenopathy suggests **toxoplasmosis**.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has fever, diarrhoea, a tender enlarged liver and crackles at the right lung base.
items.explanation: Fever with GI symptoms, **tender hepatomegaly** and **right basal crackles** suggests an **amoebic liver abscess**.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old cattle farmer has fever, weight loss and a new regurgitant murmur. Echocardiography shows an aortic valve vegetation. Three sets of blood cultures are negative after standard incubation, and he had no antibiotics beforehand.
questions.leadIn: Serology for which organism is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: True **culture-negative endocarditis** is usually caused by **fastidious** organisms: Brucella, Coxiella, Bartonella, HACEK and Tropheryma whipplei. Serology for Brucella is part of the work-up. Cattle contact and aortic valve involvement fit **Brucella endocarditis**.
whyNot: S. aureus grows readily in routine blood culture and is not diagnosed by serology.
E. coli grows readily in routine culture and is a rare cause of endocarditis.
S. pneumoniae grows in routine culture, and serology is not used to diagnose it.
Enterococci grow readily in standard blood culture.

ospe.identify: Body map of brucellosis: bone and joint lesions (suppurative arthritis, osteomyelitis, sacroiliitis, spinal spondylitis, paravertebral or psoas abscess) are the focal sites to name first.

Body map of brucellosis, other organs: nervous system (meningitis, stroke, cranial nerve palsies), eye (uveitis), heart (endocarditis), testis (epididymo-orchitis), blood (pancytopenia), and malodorous sweat as a general feature.
